entry.title: The Machine Learning “Advent Calendar” Day 8: Isolation Forest in Excel
entry.summary: Isolation Forest may look technical, but its idea is simple: isolate points using random splits. If a point is isolated quickly, it is an anomaly; if it takes many splits, it is normal. Using the tiny dataset 1, 2, 3, 9, we can see the logic clearly. We build several random trees, measure how many splits each point needs, average the depths, and convert them into anomaly scores. Short depths become scores close to 1, long depths close to 0. The Excel implementation is painful, but the algorithm itself is elegant. It scales to many features, makes no assumptions about distributions, and even works with categorical data. Above all, Isolation Forest asks a different question: not “What is normal?”, but “How fast can I isolate this point?” The post The Machine Learning “Advent Calendar” Day 8: Isolation Forest in Excel appeared first on Towards Data Science.

entry.title: How to Explore to Scale RL Training of LLMs on Hard Problems?
entry.summary: LLM RL typically operates in one of three exploration regimes: sharpening, chaining, or guided exploration; standard RL stays in the first two and plateaus on hard problems, even those in the training set. Mixing easy and hard data triggers interference, causing reward-rich tasks to drown out hard ones and stall exploration. Our approach (POPE) pushes RL into the guided regime by conditioning on prefixes from offline human data while keeping updates fully on-policy. This lets RL reliably find reward on problems previously unsolved without falling prey to the optimization issues suffered by methods that directly supervise offline traces.

entry.summary:
Published on November 11, 2025 6:20 AM GMT
Agentic sabotage occurs when an AI system intentionally takes actions that compromise safety in an environment while pursuing its own misaligned objectives. We evaluate this behavior in SHADE-Arena, a dataset for assessing sabotage and monitoring capabilities of LLM agents. We decompose agentic sabotage capability into five core components—knowing what overseers find suspicious, selecting good moments to attack, writing effective plans, strong execution, and framing suspicious actions as innocuous—which together form a scaffold that amplifies an agent’s sabotage abilities. Each component is optimized and analyzed through targeted techniques, enabled by a probabilistic model of SHADE-Arena dynamics that allows for efficient experimentation. Our tuned scaffold results in a substantial improvement in sabotage ability for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in SHADE-Arena, reducing safety score from a baseline of 0.87 to 0.41.
